Garden water

Lattice Atlas

Where can the same puddle water turn up again? Four meshes examine the garden. The Atlas brings their findings together wherever two routes meet, cross a boundary or describe the same transfer at different scales. Read the underlying path analysis.

Four meshes and what each can hide

Ground and surface water
This mesh follows water over the bank and through the soil. Calling several places “soil” can conceal different patches and depths. Reaching soil twice leaves the exact location open.
Living things
This mesh follows roots, stems, fruit, birds and snails. A leaf can hold water inside its tissue or on its surface. A shared name can create a false join between those places.
Atmosphere
This mesh follows water through evaporation, wind, dew and rain. “Air” leaves distance unspecified. The destination of rain appears only when a separate entry places a drop in the original puddle. Entry 35 and entry 36.
Built water collection
This mesh follows the roof, gutter, barrel and hose. “Garden soil” leaves the outlet location and quantity delivered unresolved. Entry 30.

Emergent pattern register

  1. Two arrivals and two exits meet at the bird

    Ground water and living things supply two arrivals. The bird can drink directly or eat fruit supplied through soil, roots and stem. Living things, soil and air supply two departures, through droppings and breath. Combining them gives four routes through the bird. The fraction of water on each remains unknown. Compare the arrivals at entry 20 and entry 21 with the departures at entry 22 and entry 23.

  2. One departure opens a route back

    Droppings put water in soil. The plant route can carry it to fruit and a bird can eat it. Reading the ground and living meshes together closes a loop. The model allows repeated trips and an exit through breath on each return. A particular bird or drop has yet to be identified. Follow entry 23, entry 7, entry 17, entry 19 and entry 20.

  3. One downstream destination has two upstream histories

    The overland and underground paths in the ground mesh both reach the same stream. If it overflows, either history can end in floodplain soil. Finding water there alone would leave both histories open. Compare entry 33 with entry 32 and their shared continuation at entry 34.

  4. A departure beyond the garden can lead back without rain

    Air carries water over the boundary. Roof dew, the gutter and the barrel bring it into the built collection mesh. The hose can deliver it to garden soil. A count confined to outward wind transport would miss this return. Follow entry 6, entry 16, entry 27, entry 28, entry 29 and entry 30.

  5. Changing the level of detail changes the count

    Compare the plant at two scales. The stem supplying developing fruit fits inside the broader plant-to-fruit description. A growing leaf likewise fits inside new growth. Adding both levels as separate physical transfers can count the same water twice. Compare entry 12 with entry 19, and entry 11 with entry 18.

What the counts mean

The first snapshot contains 16 descriptions. The second contains 36, including the original 16. Four counts the immediate puddle exits in the second snapshot. Four also counts the combinations of two arrivals and two departures at the bird. Repeated passes around the bird loop allow an unbounded number of model walks when each repetition is counted separately.

Trajectory direction declaration

  • Puddle storage · indeterminate. Repeated water volume readings are missing.
  • Soil moisture · indeterminate. Repeated measurements at a specified patch and depth are missing.
  • Streamflow · indeterminate. Repeated discharge measurements at a specified stream location are missing.

Whether the three indicators converge or diverge remains unresolved. The overall direction stays open. The snapshots document a change in the list, while change in the garden would require observations across time.
